title: Ang 1127–1135: the third and fourth Gurus
tomorrow: neither Hindu nor Muslim? what did the fifth Guru mean?

cards: Those pottery-wheel videos: a wet lump spins, two thumbs press in, and in under a minute it's a bowl. Hold that picture, because a hymn on ang 1127 does something odd with it.
It begins as a warning about pride, the pride of being born into the right family. Sharp, almost angry. And then, a few lines later, it walks into a potter's workshop.
Why would a hymn about who's higher and who's lower need a potter?

teach.h: MAHALA 3: DON'T BE PROUD OF CASTE.
teach.b: The hymn is Guru Amar Das's, the third Guru, under the heading Mahala 3. In paraphrase, it opens: don't be proud of your caste, your jaat, you fool; so many wrongs grow out of that pride.
Then it starts where people actually are: everyone talks about the four castes, it says, but all of them come from the one God. And here's the potter.

The whole world is one clay, the hymn says, and the potter shapes it into vessels of many kinds. The body is five elements put together, so who can say who's less and who's more? That's the puzzle solved.
The potter isn't decoration. He's the argument. A bowl and a jar can look nothing alike, sit on different shelves, cost different amounts.
Scrape either one and it's the same earth. Rank people by birth, and you're ranking the shape and forgetting the clay. Something to tell a friend tonight: this isn't a modern update to Sikh teaching.
It's sitting in the scripture itself, in a morning raga, in the third Guru's voice.
A few pages on, the heading turns to Mahala 4, Guru Ram Das, the fourth Guru, singing in the same raga under the same signature, Nanak. Teacher and student on neighboring pages.
Two gurus, and the same clay under both.

how: Guru Amar Das's Bhairao hymn on caste is sung in kirtan and often quoted in Sikh teaching on equality; in the gurdwara's langar, everyone sits and eats together, whatever their family.

s: it names it directly: Guru Amar Das warns against pride of caste on ang 1127.
the hymn pretends nobody talks about caste anymore
it starts from what everyone says, the four castes, then says all come from the one God.
in the hymn, the potter makes many kinds of vessels from one clay
the shape differs; the clay is the same.

games.q: at a family dinner, an aunt praises a match "because they're a good family, our kind." she turns and asks what you think. by Guru Amar Das's hymn, what's the honest reply?
o: same clay, different pots: I'd want to know what kind of person he is.
she's just proud of her family, and the hymn is fine with that kind of pride.
caste is basically gone now, so it can't matter either way.
games.why: the hymn names pride of birth and calls it the root of many wrongs, then answers it with the potter: the whole world is one clay.

practice: Pick up one thing near you that was made from earth: a mug, a plate, a flowerpot. Turn it slowly and look at it for this sit, its shape, its chips, the color under the glaze. Underneath, it's the same clay as every other pot.
If you'd like, read ang 1128 before you begin.

wordCard.voice: Ang 1127. Where Guru Amar Das, in Bhairao, warns against pride of birth and says the whole world is one clay.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: maatee, clay. the hymn says the whole world is one clay, shaped by the potter into many vessels.

carryVoice: Two gurus, one raga: the third says we're all one clay, and the fourth sings on under the same name. Day done.
